The envisaged project, therefore, provides a competitive, environmentally friendly, and sustainable BF-based process for making low-carbon emissions steel. The project has a very competitive carbon capture cost of $62.20/tonne (at an NG price of 5$ per MMBtu) while capturing 85% of CO equivalent from available BF gas. The project also produces hydrogen-rich fuel 2 gas from the BF gas, which shall be used in the powerhouse. It offers additional future optionality of being purified to produce hydrogen, which can be used in making low-carbon intensive Direct Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI). 2.0 Scope of Work Intending to design a techno-economically optimized carbon capture system, the study has aimed to design and engineer a blast furnace gas carbon capture system to reduce up to 70% CO emission from the 2 available Blast Furnace (BF) gas. A unique gas conditioning system to maximize CO concentration enabling 2 maximum CO capture from a single point, and a state-of-the-art carbon capture technology with proven 2 capture efficiencies of over 95% has been envisaged as a part of the project. The key elements of the study scope are: a) A preliminary and detailed CO capture (CC) island design. 2 b) A preliminary and detailed design of the Balance of Plant (BOP) and integration with the CC island. c) Studies and investigations include a steam and electricity sourcing study, a solvent disposal investigation, a wastewater treatment study, a permitting study and review, a hazard and operability review (HAZOP), and a constructability review. d) Detailed costing of the project, including assessing the capital cost of major equipment and the BOP, including construction costs, project indirect cost, and operating and maintenance costs. e) Report submissions include an initial engineering design and cost estimate, a techno-economic analysis (TEA), and an environmental health and safety (EH&S) risk assessment. The Water Gas 2 Shift (WGS) process is envisaged to convert the CO to CO to maximize the CO capture in this project from 2 2 available BF gas. The reactor used in this process is a high-temperature shift reactor. The steam-to-dry gas (S: DG) ratio before the high-temperature shift reactor is maintained at 0.57 as per reaction kinetics. Shift reactors are mainly deployed in oil and gas industries where stream pressure is available at high pressure and temperature. So, the WGS reactor is conventionally designed to operate at a temperature of over 608oF and a pressure above 145 psia. However, the BF gas is available for this project at low pressure of 16.7 psia, and the conditioned gas after the WGS island needs to be at low pressure for the carbon capture process.
